title: Using AI to improve recruitment of people with intellectual disabilities and autistic people to research
official: Using AI to improve recruitment of people with intellectual disabilities and autistic people to research
summary:
Background and study aims
People with learning (also called intellectual) disability and autistic people have more health problems and die at least 15 years younger than the rest of the population. To improve their health outcomes, we need to know what treatments work for them. This is usually done through clinical trials. However, we know that up to 90% of clinical trials, where people are allocated to either receive or not receive a treatment by chance (called randomisation) do not include people with learning disability or autism. This means we cannot be sure that treatments tested in people without learning disability or autism, will be appropriate for them.  

Aims of this research: Improve understanding of clinical trial information and support informed decision-making about research participation among people with intellectual disabilities (ID) and autistic people. We aim to do this by developing an artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to explain research studies in a clear and accessible way and answer people’s questions. 

Who can participate?
Adults with intellectual disability or autistic adults

What does the study involve?
We will speak to people with learning disability, autistic people, their carers and researchers about using an AI chatbot to improve understanding of clinical trials and help them to decide to take part. We will use this information to design and improve the AI chatbot.  We will then test the AI chatbot in a small study. Around 10 people with learning disability and 10 autistic people will use the chatbot to learn about a clinical trial. We will record and analyse data from these interactions. We will also ask participants what they thought about it. We will ask clinical trial experts to use the AI chatbot and give their feedback. We will use what we have learnt to further improve the AI chatbot. 

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
No risks to participating in this study except for the person does not enjoying or getting bored by the AI chatbot. No specific benefits except that the person learns about what AI chatbots can do and how to operate them. 

Where is the study run from?
University College London (UK).

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
July 2026 to June 2028.

Who is funding the study?
National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) (UK). 

Who is the main contact? 
Bhathika Perera, b.perera@ucl.ac.uk
conditions: Increase understanding and recruitment of people with intellectual disability or autistic people into clinical trials using an AI chatbot
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Adults with intellectual disability and autistic adults, with carers where appropriate who are able to consent to participate in the study. This study registration is for the UK arm of the study as this study is also replicated in South Korea.
Exclusion criteria:
1. Any clinical, communication, safeguarding or other circumstance in which the research team judges that participation cannot be conducted safely despite reasonable adjustments
2. Cannot provide informed consent
